narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 57.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is not a certainty, but it means failure was judged more likely than passage, so the school treated your application as too risky to admit.

The strongest factor was your LSAT score. At 38, it was slightly above the accepted-student average of 37.18, and this factor pushed the prediction toward passing. However, two other factors outweighed it. Your third-year class-rank decile was 4, compared with an average of 5.79 among accepted students, and it was the second most influential factor; it pushed toward bar failure, suggesting your later academic standing was weaker than that of admitted students. Your undergraduate GPA, 2.70 versus an accepted average of 3.23, was the third most important factor and also pushed toward failure. Family income and full-time status were not among the top influences.

To improve a future application, focus on the areas that raised concern: complete additional rigorous coursework to raise your GPA, seek academic support or a post-baccalaureate/graduate program to show improved performance, and if possible strengthen your third-year academic record before applying again. You may also retake the LSAT if you can improve further, but your GPA and academic trend need the most attention. Ask admissions for feedback and submit updated transcripts if you continue coursework.
